screens.title: Functions (Methods) and Parameters
screens.subtitle: Break code into reusable tools, pass data, and return results with clear scope and form.

narration.text: In this chapter we learn how to turn repeated game logic into named, reusable tools called methods. Methods let you package a behavior — like applying damage, spawning items, or calculating experience — behind a clear name and a concise list of inputs and outputs. You’ll see how parameters accept values from a caller, how return types send calculated results back, and how overloading gives you multiple ways to perform the same conceptual action. We’ll also cover variable scope so you won’t accidentally access a local variable from outside its method, and we’ll contrast instance methods that act on a specific object with static methods like Unity’s Mathf utilities. By the end you should be able to refactor a bloated Start method into small focused methods, choose when to return a value versus changing state, and avoid common mistakes like using instance data inside static methods. As you follow the code examples, ask yourself where a repeated line of logic in your project could become a method — that’s where real maintainability begins.

keyIdea.title: Why methods matter
keyIdea.text: Methods encapsulate behavior, accept arguments, and optionally return values so your scripts stay readable, testable, and reusable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Functions Overview
Make your code modular and predictable

Methods let you name behavior, accept inputs, return results, and keep game logic easy to follow. This chapter focuses on definitions, calls, parameters, return types, overloading, and scope in Unity C#.

In this lesson

Define functions to encapsulate behavior and pass values in.

Coming up

Design multiple signatures and return computed values.

Practice

Understand where variables live and when to use static methods.

Visual concept
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Method

A named block that performs a task and can be reused any time that task is needed.

Inputs via parameters. Optional output via return.
Parameters

Placeholders that receive data when a method is called. They make methods flexible.

Called with arguments.
Return

A method can send a result back using a return type. Use this when the caller needs a value.

Use return carefully to avoid side effects.
Scope

Where a variable can be accessed. Member fields are accessible to methods; local variables are not.

Avoid referencing out-of-scope variables.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will gain and how to measure them

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define and call your own methods, pass values into methods via parameters, and receive values back with return types. You will learn to implement method overloading so a single action name can have multiple signatures, which keeps code intent clear while supporting different input scenarios. Another goal is to understand variable scope: knowing which variables are local to a method and which are member fields prevents common errors where code tries to access a name that doesn’t exist in that context. Finally, you will distinguish between instance methods, which act on a specific object, and static methods, which belong to a class and are called by name. These skills are practical: they let you refactor long Start or Update methods into testable, reusable pieces, and they prevent runtime errors caused by scope or incorrect method calls.

keyIdea.text: Define, call, overload, and reason about methods and scope; design when to return values versus updating state.

screens.title: What you'll practice
screens.subtitle: Concrete tasks to demonstrate each objective

narration.text: To make these objectives concrete you will refactor a bloated Start method into smaller functions, create overloaded methods to handle different call patterns, and write a method that returns a value for use in other logic. You will also run a small experiment: attach a utility script to a GameObject, change inspector fields, and observe console messages to verify which overload executed and whether scope rules held. The practice tasks show why choosing between returning a value and changing a field matters: returned values keep functions pure and predictable, while direct state changes are useful when the method should update the object it belongs to. Finally, you'll spot and fix two common errors: attempting to access a method-local variable from another method, and calling an instance method without an object reference. These exercises will lock in the difference between static and instance methods and give you hands-on confidence.

screens.title: What is a Method?
screens.subtitle: A named block that performs a specific task and can be reused

narration.text: A method is a named, self-contained block of code that performs a single task. Methods improve readability and let you reuse logic across a script or even across projects. For example, instead of writing damage calculations directly inside Start or Update, you write a method named TakeDamage that accepts a damage parameter and updates player health. That single name tells other developers what happens and hides implementation details. A good method has a clear responsibility, a concise parameter list, and either updates state or returns a value, but not both unnecessarily. As a concrete example from Unity scripts, you might implement public void TakeDamage(float damage) to deduct health and call Die() when health reaches zero. A common misconception is thinking a method is only for returning values — methods are equally useful when they perform actions like disabling a GameObject. Finally, ask yourself: would this code be easier to test or reuse if it were in a method? If yes, extract it. What is a Method? means methods encapsulate a single, reusable behavior and improve code clarity and maintainability.. In practical terms, a named block that performs a specific task and can be reused. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Method definition
keyIdea.text: Methods encapsulate a single, reusable behavior and improve code clarity and maintainability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is a Method?
Definition & importance

A method packages behavior into a named unit. This reduces repetition, clarifies intent, and makes testing and maintenance easier.

When to extract
If you repeat code or a block does one coherent thing, extract it into a method with a clear name and parameters instead of duplicating logic.
Common mistake
Putting too many responsibilities into one method makes reuse hard. Prefer small methods with focused purpose.
Key Takeaway

Name behavior clearly and keep methods focused so they can be reused and tested independently.

Code example
public void TakeDamage(float damage)
{
    playerHealth -= damage;
    Debug.Log("Player took " + damage + " damage. Current health: " + playerHealth);

    if (playerHealth <= 0)
    {
        Die();
    }
}
This method shows a simple pattern: accept input, update state, and call another method if a condition is met. Ask: does this method have a single responsibility?
Analogy
Think of a method as a single tool on a workbench. You reach for the tool when you need its task done; you don’t rebuild the tool each time.

screens.title: Anatomy of a C# Method
screens.subtitle: Return type, name, parameters, and body

narration.text: A method has four visible parts: a return type, a name, a parameter list, and a body that executes when called. The return type can be void to indicate no value is returned, or it can be a data type such as float or int when the method computes a result. Parameters are declared inside parentheses and define the types and names of input data the method expects. For example, public float CalculateTotalDamage(float baseDamage, float criticalMultiplier) declares a method that returns a float and takes two float parameters. Inside the body you compute a result and use the return keyword to send that value back to the caller. A typical misconception is thinking the return keyword also updates members automatically — it does not. A return value is just data the caller receives; it will only change object state if you assign that return to a field or use it in a method that updates state. Practice: when you need a computed number for later logic, prefer returning it; when you need to change the object directly, use void and modify fields inside the method.

keyIdea.title: Method parts
keyIdea.text: Return type, name, parameters, and body define what a method accepts and provides; choose return vs side-effect intentionally.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Anatomy of a Method
Parts explained
  • Return type: What type the method gives back, or void for none.
  • Name: The identifier others use to call the behavior.
  • Parameters: Typed names the method expects when called.
  • Body: The statements that perform the work.
Common misconception

You cannot overload methods by only changing the return type. The compiler needs different parameter lists to choose an overload.

Code walkthrough
public float CalculateTotalDamage(float baseDamage, float criticalMultiplier)
{
    float totalDamage = baseDamage * criticalMultiplier;
    return totalDamage;
}
This method returns a computed float. The caller stores that return value to use in further calculations or to pass to another method.
Example use
float criticalHit = CalculateTotalDamage(10f, 1.5f); Debug.Log("A critical hit would deal: " + criticalHit);

screens.title: Calling Methods and Passing Arguments
screens.subtitle: How arguments map to parameters and change behavior at runtime

narration.text: When you call a method you provide arguments that map to the method’s parameters. The parameter is a named placeholder in the method definition; the argument is the actual value you pass in at runtime. For example, calling TakeDamage(attackDamage) passes whatever value attackDamage currently holds into the parameter named damage inside the method. This means the same method can behave differently on each call depending on the argument values. A frequent source of confusion is the difference between passing a literal value and passing a variable; both are valid arguments. Another important point is that parameters receive copies of values for value types; changing the parameter inside the method does not change the caller’s variable unless you intentionally return a new value or use references. In Unity, you often pass Vector3 positions, floats for damage or speed, or GameObject references. Practice: call the same overload with different arguments or use a literal to confirm how the method behaves when fed different inputs. Calling Methods and Passing Arguments means parameters name expected inputs; arguments are the actual values you pass when calling the method.. In practical terms, how arguments map to parameters and change behavior at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Parameters vs Arguments
keyIdea.text: Parameters name expected inputs; arguments are the actual values you pass when calling the method.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Calling Methods
Parameter mapping
A parameter declares a type and name. When you call the method, the argument’s value is assigned to that parameter for the duration of the call.
Example calls
TakeDamage(attackDamage);
TakeDamage(5.0f);
float crit = CalculateTotalDamage(attackDamage, 1.5f);
Misconception
Passing a variable name means the method receives its current value — not a magic link. Unless you use reference types intentionally, methods receive copies of the values for primitives.
Quick checklist
  • Match argument types to parameter types to avoid compiler errors.
  • Use literals for quick tests and variables for dynamic behavior.
  • Remember that return values must be stored if you need them later.
Key Takeaway

Arguments control runtime behavior; parameters define what a method accepts. Choose types and names that make intent clear.

screens.title: Method Overloading
screens.subtitle: Multiple signatures for the same conceptual action

narration.text: Method overloading lets you provide several methods with the same name but different parameter lists, so the same conceptual action can be called in different ways. For example, three SpawnItem overloads let you spawn a default item by position, spawn a specified prefab by position, or spawn with a specific rotation. The compiler chooses which overload to call based on the number and types of arguments you pass. A common mistake is thinking you can overload only by changing the return type; the compiler will not accept two methods that differ only by return type. Overloading improves ergonomics: the caller uses the simplest call when defaults are fine, and a more detailed overload when extra control is needed. As a concrete example, SpawnItem(new Vector3(0,0,0)) will call the single-argument overload, while SpawnItem(rareItemPrefab, position) matches the two-argument overload. Overloading helps keep a single conceptual method name for related behaviors while offering flexible interfaces. Method Overloading means overloaded methods must differ by parameter list (types, number, or order); return type alone is not enough.. In practical terms, multiple signatures for the same conceptual action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Overloading rule
keyIdea.text: Overloaded methods must differ by parameter list (types, number, or order); return type alone is not enough.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Method Overloading
Why overload?

Overloading gives callers convenience while keeping the conceptual action name consistent. Each overload handles different input requirements.

Example overloads
public void SpawnItem(Vector3 position)
public void SpawnItem(GameObject itemPrefab, Vector3 position)
public void SpawnItem(GameObject itemPrefab, Vector3 position, Quaternion rotation)
Gotcha
You cannot create two methods that only differ by return type. The signatures must be different in parameters.
Call resolution

The compiler selects the overload that matches the types and number of arguments you pass. If multiple overloads could match, choose the most specific one to avoid ambiguity.

Key Takeaway

Use overloading to offer convenient, related ways to perform the same action without duplicating names or intent.

screens.title: Variable Scope
screens.subtitle: Where variables are valid and the errors that arise when they are not

narration.text: Variable scope defines where you can read or write a variable. Member variables, also called fields, are declared at the class level and are accessible to every method in that class. Local variables are declared inside a method and exist only while that method is running. In the ScopeExample, classLevelVariable is a member and can be read by MyMethod1 and MyMethod2. By contrast, methodLevelVariable exists only inside MyMethod1; attempting to access it from MyMethod2 causes a compile-time error. A common error is accidentally shadowing a member with a local variable of the same name; this hides the field and can create confusing behavior. Another pitfall is assuming a return value modifies a member when it only returns a copy; you must assign returned values to fields if you want to persist them. To avoid scope bugs, give local variables descriptive names and prefer fields only when state genuinely needs to persist across method calls. Finally, test by attempting to reference a local variable from another method — the compiler will guide you to the correct design. Variable Scope means member fields are accessible to all methods in the class; local variables live only inside the method where they are declared.. In practical terms, where variables are valid and the errors that arise when they are not. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope rules
keyIdea.text: Member fields are accessible to all methods in the class; local variables live only inside the method where they are declared.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Variable Scope
Scope explained

Fields declared at class level persist across method calls. Local variables are temporary and exist only during the method execution.

Example
public int classLevelVariable = 10;

void MyMethod1()
{
    int methodLevelVariable = 5;
    Debug.Log(classLevelVariable);
}

void MyMethod2()
{
    Debug.Log(classLevelVariable);
    // methodLevelVariable is not accessible here
}
Common error

Trying to use a method-local variable outside its method will fail at compile time. Move it to a field if multiple methods need it.

Design guidance
  • Use local variables for temporary calculations.
  • Use fields for state that must persist across calls or be visible in the Inspector.
  • Avoid name shadowing; it confuses both you and the compiler.
Check your understanding
If a value must be preserved between frames, where should it be declared? (Answer: as a field.)

screens.title: Static vs Instance Methods
screens.subtitle: When to call methods on a class vs an object instance

narration.text: Static methods belong to a class and are called using the class name, while instance methods act on a specific object and can access that object’s fields. In Unity, Mathf. Abs or Mathf. Clamp are examples of static methods: you call Mathf. Abs(-10.5f) without creating an instance of Mathf. In contrast, methods on a MonoBehaviour are usually instance methods because they operate on that particular component’s state, for example TakeDamage modifies this player’s health field. A common pitfall is trying to access instance variables from a static method — that won’t work because a static method has no this reference. Another design choice is to make utility functions static when they don’t require object state; this makes them convenient helpers. Use instance methods when the operation should modify or read instance-specific data. As a practical check, if your method needs access to inspector values on the component, implement it as an instance method; if not, a static utility may be cleaner and clearer. Static vs Instance Methods means static methods are class-level utilities; instance methods operate on specific object state and can use the this reference.. In practical terms, when to call methods on a class vs an object instance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Static vs Instance
keyIdea.text: Static methods are class-level utilities; instance methods operate on specific object state and can use the this reference.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Static vs Instance
Static examples
float absoluteValue = Mathf.Abs(-10.5f);
float clampedValue = Mathf.Clamp(15f, 0f, 10f);

Mathf methods are static utilities. You don’t create a Mathf instance to use them.

When to use static
Use static for pure utilities that don’t need object state, like math helpers or conversion functions.
Instance examples
public void TakeDamage(float damage)
{
    playerHealth -= damage; // uses this instance's field
}

Instance methods can access fields and modify the specific component they belong to.

Mistake to avoid

Don’t call instance members from a static method. If you need instance state, make the method an instance method instead.

screens.title: Refactoring Start into Methods
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step approach to extract behavior into methods

narration.text: Refactoring a large Start method into smaller methods is a practical way to apply the ideas in this chapter. Start by identifying distinct behaviors in Start: initialization, applying damage, computing bonuses, and spawning items. Extract each behavior into a clearly named method such as Initialize(), TakeDamage(float amount), CalculateExperience(int enemyLevel), and SpawnItem variants. Replace the original code with calls to these methods. When extracting, decide whether the new method should return a value or modify fields: return a value when the caller needs a result to proceed; modify fields when the method is responsible for changing the object’s state. After extraction, run the scene and confirm console logs and behavior remain correct. A useful pattern is to write small unit-like tests by calling the methods in isolation with known inputs and inspecting console output. Finally, remember to keep parameter lists concise; if a method needs many parameters, it may signal an opportunity to group data into a struct or class. Refactoring improves readability and makes future changes far safer. Refactoring Start into Methods means extract coherent behaviors into named methods, choosing return vs side-effect based on who should own the state change.. In practical terms, a step-by-step approach to extract behavior into methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor rules
keyIdea.text: Extract coherent behaviors into named methods, choosing return vs side-effect based on who should own the state change.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Refactor Start
Step-by-step
  1. Identify distinct responsibilities in Start.
  2. Create small methods with descriptive names and minimal parameters.
  3. Choose return vs modify: return values when the caller needs results.
  4. Replace inlined code with calls and run tests to verify behavior.
Pro tip
Extract methods one at a time and run the scene after each extraction. This keeps debugging simple and ensures you catch regressions quickly.
Refactor example
// Before: large Start method
// After: calls to extracted methods
void Start()
{
    Initialize();
    TakeDamage(attackDamage);
    float xp = CalculateExperience(enemyLevel);
    Debug.Log("XP: " + xp);
}
This pattern keeps Start readable and delegates the details to well-named methods. The console output remains a reliable verification step after each change.

screens.title: PlayerUtility Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Implement overloads, a return-value method, and a critical hit check

narration.text: The PlayerUtility script from the hands-on activity ties many chapter concepts together. It defines ApplyDamage overloads to show different call patterns, a CalculateFinalDamage method that returns a float, and a CheckForCriticalHit method that returns a boolean. When you attach the script to a GameObject and run the scene, the Console prints messages that reveal which overload executed and whether a critical hit occurred. For example, ApplyDamage(amount) logs a normal hit, while ApplyDamage(amount, true) logs a critical hit after doubling the damage inside the method. The CalculateFinalDamage method shows how a method can compute and return a number without changing fields, demonstrating local variable scope. CheckForCriticalHit uses Random. Range to return a boolean indicating a critical event; treat Random as a black box for now and focus on how the method returns true or false. A common misconception is expecting the return of CalculateFinalDamage to modify the object automatically; remember to assign the returned value to a field if you want it saved. After running, experiment by changing baseDamage and criticalChance in the Inspector to see different console flows. PlayerUtility Walkthrough means combining overloads, returns, and randomness in a utility script demonstrates how these concepts interoperate in real code.. In practical terms, implement overloads, a return-value method, and a critical hit check. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Integrated practice
keyIdea.text: Combining overloads, returns, and randomness in a utility script demonstrates how these concepts interoperate in real code.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › PlayerUtility Walkthrough
What to observe
  • Which ApplyDamage overload printed which message.
  • Whether CalculateFinalDamage returned the expected number without modifying fields.
  • How CheckForCriticalHit returns true based on a random threshold and affects which overload is called.
Experiment
Tweak baseDamage and criticalChance in the Inspector and rerun Play mode to observe different console messages and critical outcomes.
Example code snippet
// Method that returns a value
public float CalculateFinalDamage(float baseVal, float multiplier)
{
    float finalDamage = baseVal * multiplier;
    return finalDamage; // local variable returned
}
Notice how finalDamage exists only inside the method. The caller stores the return to use it later. This shows local scope and clear return semantics in practice.

screens.title: MethodPuzzle: Predict the Console Output
screens.subtitle: Walk through execution order, return values, and side effects

narration.text: Consider a class with a private score field, an AddPoints method that updates the field and logs the current score, and a GetDoubleScore method that returns twice the current score. When Start calls AddPoints(10), then GetDoubleScore, then AddPoints(5), walk through the state changes carefully. Initially score is zero. AddPoints(10) updates the field to ten and logs that current score. GetDoubleScore computes and returns twenty, but it doesn’t change the original score field — it only returns a value. The log showing the doubled result prints twenty. Finally AddPoints(5) increases the score field to fifteen and logs the updated field. A common misconception is believing GetDoubleScore will alter the persisted score because its return is larger; it doesn’t unless the code assigns that return back to the field. The correct console sequence demonstrates how returns and side effects differ and why understanding both is essential for debugging. MethodPuzzle: Predict the Console Output means a method that returns a value does not automatically change object state; side-effects must be explicit.. In practical terms, walk through execution order, return values, and side effects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Execution vs Return
keyIdea.text: A method that returns a value does not automatically change object state; side-effects must be explicit.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › MethodPuzzle
Puzzle code
private int _score = 0;

void AddPoints(int points)
{
    _score += points;
    Debug.Log("Current score after adding: " + _score);
}

int GetDoubleScore()
{
    int doubled = _score * 2;
    return doubled;
}

void Start()
{
    AddPoints(10);
    int finalScore = GetDoubleScore();
    Debug.Log("Final doubled score: " + finalScore);
    AddPoints(5);
}
Step-through & answer
  1. After AddPoints(10) the field is 10. Console prints current score 10.
  2. GetDoubleScore returns 20 but does not change _score; finalScore is 20 and prints.
  3. AddPoints(5) sets _score to 15 and prints current score 15.
Reflection
Why might returning a computed value instead of modifying a field be preferable for testability?

screens.title: Design Patterns for Methods
screens.subtitle: When to return vs modify, naming, and parameter design

narration.text: Choosing whether a method should return a value or modify object state is a design decision with practical consequences. Prefer returning values when the operation is a pure computation that doesn’t need to persist changes to the object — this makes the method easier to test and reason about. Use void methods that modify fields when the purpose is to change the object’s state, such as disabling a GameObject on death. Naming matters: pick verb phrases that reflect intent, like CalculateFinalDamage for a computation and ApplyDamage when the method mutates state. Keep parameter lists short and meaningful; many parameters suggest grouping data into a small data structure or using a class field if data is shared across calls. Another useful pattern is to provide an overload with fewer parameters that uses sensible defaults, and a more detailed overload for full control. A common pitfall is making utility methods instance methods when they do not require instance data — prefer static for pure utilities to clarify intent and simplify calls. Design Patterns for Methods means return values for pure computations; void instance methods for state changes; name and parameter lists to convey intent.. In practical terms, when to return vs modify, naming, and parameter design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design decisions
keyIdea.text: Return values for pure computations; void instance methods for state changes; name and parameter lists to convey intent.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Method Design
Practical rules
  • Return values for pure calculations; avoid hidden side-effects.
  • Name methods to reveal their behavior: Calculate, Apply, Spawn, Check, Get.
  • Use overloads to provide convenient defaults and detailed control.
  • Keep parameter lists short; group related data when it grows.
Key Takeaway

Design methods with clarity: intent, inputs, outputs, and lifetime should be obvious from the signature and name.

Analogy
Method signatures are contracts.

The parameter list and return type tell callers what to supply and what to expect back — treat them as a small API contract for the method.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to keep while coding

narration.text: Remember three core ideas as you write methods. First, a method is a single, named block of code designed for reuse; extract repeated logic into a method with a clear verb-based name. Second, parameters and return types define the input and output contract; pass arguments to match parameter types and return computed values when you need to preserve functional purity. Third, scope and method type matter: member fields persist across methods, local variables do not, and static methods cannot access instance state. Keep these reminders close while refactoring: they help you choose when to return a value versus modifying state, when to use overloads for convenience, and how to avoid common scope errors. Use small, testable methods to make your Unity scripts predictable and maintainable. Key Concepts means methods encapsulate behavior; parameters define inputs; scope determines visibility and side-effects.. In practical terms, three compact reminders to keep while coding. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Key Concepts
Method (Function)
A named block for a single, reusable behavior.
Parameters & Return
Parameters accept inputs; return types give back computed results to the caller.
Scope & Static
Fields persist across methods; locals are temporary. Static methods have no instance context.
Summary
Design methods for clear inputs, predictable outputs, and minimal side-effects. Favor small, testable methods to keep your Unity scripts maintainable.

narration.text: Keep these short definitions at hand as you write code. A method is a named block performing a specific task. The return type describes what the method gives back, and void means nothing is returned. Parameters are the declared inputs that accept arguments when called. Method overloading provides multiple signatures for one conceptual action and is resolved by the compiler using argument types and counts. Variable scope tells you where a variable is visible: local to a method or shared as a member field. Static methods belong to the class and cannot access instance fields, while instance methods operate on a specific object. These concise definitions will help you reason quickly while refactoring and debugging in Unity.
